analytic.title: Empirical Bounds of Multicore Cache Interference for Real-Time Schedulability Analysis

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Multicore processors offer significant advantages of weight, power, and space to embedded real-time developers, making their adoption almost inevitable. Also, system sustainability and economies of scale will increasingly make multicore devices indispensable. However, predictability of performance, specifically, establishing realistic upper bounds on execution time for schedulability analysis is a significant challenge to certification. This paper describes a methodology for empirically establishing a reasonable, high-confidence upper bound for cache interference effects in the context of engineering practices commonly used in certifiable real-time systems.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Embedded computing has long relied on Rate Monotonic Analysis (RMA), ARINC 653, or similar methods to guarantee that all real-time tasks receive enough execution bandwidth to complete. Showing that this property holds provides critical evidence for most safety or airworthiness certification processes [1], [2]. Effective use of RMA depends on knowing the maximum or worst-case execution time for every task in the real-time system. For many years, this could be measured once on the computer, and as long as the code for the real-time tasks did not change, and was written such that the execution behavior is predictable (e.g., without garbage collection or stochastic algorithms), the execution times would be stable and predictable.

Changes in computer architecture from the 1980's through today have chipped away at this predictability. Innovations like pipelined architectures, out-of-order execution, and multiple levels of cache memory have made measurements of execution time dependent on factors other than the code. Effectively, this has made low-level resource dispatching approaches less "priority-based" and more "fairness-based". Even so, real-time practitioners have discovered ways to apply RMA effectively, through techniques like measuring execution times multiple times and selecting the maximum observation, and remeasuring all tasks when any significant changes in the code base occur, since the execution time of one task can influence the execution times of other tasks.

As multicore processors become increasingly considered within critical applications such as aircraft or automobiles, the timing interdependence of individual, logically independent task execution times becomes impossible to ignore. In most multicore architectures, each core has one or two relatively small cache memories dedicated for use by that core, and a much larger last-level cache (LLC) that is shared by all cores in the processor. It is the impact of the LLC on task execution times that makes measuring the worst-case execution times for real-time tasks so difficult. While practitioners can attempt to measure task times with all other tasks on the other cores executing, guaranteeing that the measured times truly capture worst-case behavior is not possible under loaded conditions.

Constructing a purely analytical model of multicore cache is too complex, may be too pessismistic and may give rise to un-necessarily high engineering margins. We can instead establish empirical worst-case performance envelopes for a variety of application sizes, and use that information to produce reasonable upper bounds for worst-case performance. Changes to the underlying hardware, software or application behavior, as suggested by prior literature in this area, may not always be practical, especially when re-hosting existing applications. In contrast, the methodology presented in this paper does not require such modifications, and relies on an interference characterization to be constructed once for a given multicore platform. The proposed method is also generic, and can be used with project-specific hardware and software. This paper describes a methodology for empirically establishing a reasonable, high-confidence upper bound for cache interference effects in the context of engineering practices commonly used in certifiable real-time systems. Our approach is based on characterizing a multidimensional parameter space that can affect the performance of shared caches. We describe a test bed and testing approach, including tool-based support for semi-exhaustive testing within the multidimensional space and thereby establish platform characterization for cache interference. Preliminary results indicate that cache interference is more sensitive to certain parameters such as application memory size and number of cores loaded. Once established, this characterization is then used to (a) locate a given application configuration within the cache interference stress bounds, thus estimating available safety margins; (b) calculate adjustments needed to worst-case execution times for performance analysis; and (c) guide application resource allocation while taking cache interference into account.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: section II discusses previous and related work; section III describes the effects of interference on real-time predictability; in section IV we outline our experimental setup and measurement methodology; results are presented in sections V; VI suggests potential application; VII the conclusion, and VIII future work.

div.head: II. PRIOR WORK
div.p: Prior work in this area generally falls into four approaches: analysis of application behavior to develop an analytic bound on cache interference, application modification to improve reference locality, operating system controls to improve performance or enforce limits, and using features in the underlying hardware to ease the effects of cache interference. In each of these areas, we discuss papers which best typify the work in that area.

div.head: Analytical bounding
div.p: The work by Subramanian [3], [4], [5] shows a leading result to quantify inter-application interference effects of shared cache interference on multicore systems. In contrast to application-aware memory scheduling, Subramanian proposes two analytic models: Memory Interference induced Slowdown Estimation (MISE) Model and an Application Slowdown Model (ASM). While MISE does not take shared caches into account, ASM does by exploiting two observations: that the performance of a memory-bound application is roughly proportional to the rate at which it accesses shared cache and that the stand-alone/no-interference request-rate of an application can be estimated based on its highest priority requests in accessing memory. ASM quantifies shared cache interference in terms of the number of misses that would have been hits if the application did not share the cache with other applications (contention misses). Aggregate contention misses combined with the average miss service time is used to estimate the actual time it would have taken to serve the application's requests had it been run alone.

div.head: Application modification
div.p: Wolf and Lam [9] present one of the landmark results in modifying applications to improve their reference locality, by analyzing memory references and attempting to co-locate temporally close memory operations to as few hardware cache lines as possible, thus satisfying more memory accesses with fewer cache line misses. Such an approach is probably best applied as guidelines during application development and coding, since the cost required to apply it to already-certified code is likely prohibitive. Kansakar and Munir [7] develop an approach where parameters such as cache line misses can be used to explore the space of potential allocations of applications to processor cores. Using a greedy search algorithm, their work provides an optimized allocation which tries to reduce shared cache interference. However, this valuable work leaves unanswered the development of bounds on cache interference. Gunther et al. [8] similarly propose an application-level methodology for tuning multicore performance with a focus on scalability of multithreaded applications; this work is focused on enterprise, web service-class applications.

div.head: Operating system controls
div.p: Yun et al. [10] develop real-time operating system controls for actively allocating memory and cache bandwidth provide guaranteed bandwidth to critical applications. While demonstrated to be useful when shared cache competition is so intense that critical applications could be starved, it does not directly address the problem of ensuring that all applications in the processor can execute correctly.

An alternative approach is presented in Ward et al. [12], which relies on coloring cache demands by application, then scheduling to minimize or eliminate contention for shared cache. While the work is significant, the overheads involved in its current implementation may limit its use in safety-critical real-time embedded environments; the paper reports overheads of 400μs-900μs for switching between applications.

div.head: Hardware-supported allocation
div.p: Most modern processor manufacturers offer facilities that try to minimize the impacts of LLC interference, such as described by Herdrich [11]. Such approaches can indeed deliver useful results, guaranteeing execution times for selected tasks at the cost of increasing execution times for other tasks. In addition, these can be problematic to implement in practice on an extremely large code base, as the analysis required to identify the right set of cache lines to lock is very difficult.

div.head: III. WHY CONSIDER INTERFERENCE EFFECTS
div.p: Figure 1 shows an 8-core processor in which each core possesses dedicated (private) L1 and L2 caches, and shares a much larger L3 cache with the other cores. The left side shows the case where the applications on Core 0 are executing using a large percentage of the L3 cache. In this case, the Core 0 applications will experience best-case execution times, since all of its memory references will be satisfied by cache hits, the fastest possible execution behavior. On the right, we show the same Core 0 applications executing with significant competition from the applications running on Cores 1-7. In this new case, since Core 0 is forced to use much less L3 cache, a larger percentage of its memory references will have to come from main memory, introducing significant execution time delays.

In general, once Core 0's memory usage exceeds the sum of private L1 and L2 cache sizes, its performance depends on its ability to maintain its excess memory needs in the L3 cache. With increased competition from the other cores for L3 cache space, Core 0's applications will experience more frequent delays for main memory references, which are many times the access speed for cached memory. The impact on Core 0's execution times is a function of its total memory reference pattern (size and frequency) and the memory reference patterns of its competition (Cores 1-7).

The reason embedded real-time software architects should be concerned about this is the need to closely bound the worstcase execution times for every application running on the processor. As we show in this paper, the worst-case execution times for real-time applications depend on each core's memory usage pattern, and the aggregate of these patterns determines L3 cache competition. For embedded avionics systems, the ability to establish an upper bound for the worst-case execution times of these safety-and mission-critical real-time systems is key in demonstrating their airworthiness to certifying authorities.

Constructing a purely analytical model is too complex, and thus too expensive for practitioners. We can instead establish empirical worst-case performance envelopes for a variety of application sizes, and use that information to produce upper bounds for worst-case performance.

div.head: A. Experiment Parameters
div.p: In this work, we seek to establish high-confidence upper bounds for cache interference effects when using multicore platforms. Our experiment design seeks to saturate resource contention via parameter exploration, and thereby establish boundaries for resource saturation. Although artificial rather than application-induced saturation, this forced saturation via exploration results in a higher confidence in the upper bound. To simplify the combinatorial explosion from the parameter space exploration, we assume that the applications are designed without dynamic memory usage and garbage collectors, and with stable, non-stochastic execution behavior, with hard realtime constraints.

In the presence of interference due to shared memory cache usage, we expect that the performance of an application depends on the following parameters: (a) its own and other applications' memory usage pattern, (b) processor utilization pattern of the applications and, (c) the processor clock speed. These parameters are therefore selected for experimentation.

Memory usage pattern components are: memory size, memory usage intensity, read-write mix, and access direction mix. The processor utilization pattern components are: number of threads, thread periods, and their execution times. These components are briefly explained below. The valid ranges and the specific values used in our experiments are listed in the next section.

Memory size represents the data memory being used by the application. Since the typical avionics application is not codeintensive (i.e., relatively compact code that does repetitive processing on large amounts of data), we decided to limit our exploration to data memory.

Memory usage intensity, or Stride, represents the intensity with which the application steps through the memory, with higher values implying higher stress on the cache subsystem. A stride of 1, where the consumption routine reads/writes every value in each cache line, makes maximum use of, for example, a 16-unit cache line once it has been loaded. While a cache miss may be triggered by reference to the first value in the line, the subsequent 15 references should all be hits since the cache line has been loaded following the first miss, yielding faster execution time and lower pressure on the memory subsystem. On the other hand, a stride of 8 will reference only 2 values in the cache line, so the processor will be able to take advantage of only 1 cache hit before moving into the following cache line. This generates references to cache lines in quicker succession, yielding higher memory subsystem stress.

Read-write mix represents the mix of read and write accesses to the memory by the application, indicated as a percent of read accesses. We expected, and observed, higher memory subsystem stress with higher write fractions.

Direction mix represents the mix of forward vs. backward memory accesses. Although the exact behavior is machinespecific, in general forward address motion may take less time to execute than backward, since pre-fetch usually works in the forward direction.

Processor utilization pattern components are the number of threads, thread periods and execution times. An application consists of the specified number of threads, their periods and execution times. Aggregate application utilization can be derived from these three components.

Processor clock speed is typically fixed at configuration and never changed in high-integrity avionics applications. We expected that this setting may have impact on the movement of data from memory to cache and to the cores, and hence included this as an independent variable in our experiments. To measure the relative impact of each of the above different factors on the cache interference, we decided to vary each of them independently, thus generating a highdimensional dataset, which can then be sliced to study each parameter's effect in isolation, or in combination with others.

div.head: B. Experiment Hardware and Software
div.p: Figure 2 shows our experimentation platform hardware and software. The methodology described herein is generic and can be adapted to most other hardware or software elements. It is important to use a real-time operating system supporting preemptive fixed priority scheduling, and tracing software capable of capturing kernel context switches so that application execution times can be computed from trace logs. In order to develop and execute the interference parameter set described in Table 1 below, we utilized the nForge software, currently in private beta. nForge is a rule-based software platform for model integration [13]. nForge was used to automate the generation of load using selected parameters, download it to the hardware platform, execute it, gather trace data and extract execution times, and transform the data to a form suitable for analysis and discussion.

The number of threads, thread frequency and thread execution times were chosen in such combination that the total baseline processor utilization (without any interference) was always approximately 60%. The product of total count of experiment values (equal to 97200) represents the number of experiments to execute for parameter space exploration. We used the nTrace load generator to generate a specified amount of execution time, given the various component values of memory usage pattern, processor usage pattern and processor speed. This load generator uses a configuration file which is generated by a calibration process. Calibration consists of measuring test runs under a near-exhaustive set of combinations. Given this resulting set of measurements, we can interpolate with high accuracy to yield an iteration count to run a particular test to achieve a desired execution time.

In our experimentation, we intentionally included stresses due to overloading well beyond what a reasonable engineering judgment would allow for. This high forced saturation employed is intentionally non-realistic, as we intend to capture the upper limit boundaries, seen on the interference characterization plots to be extremely conservative. This philosophy is consistent with the underpinnings of Rate-Monotic Analysis and helps to establish confidence needed in satisfying critical function certification criteria -which requires erring on any inherent uncertainty on the conservative side.

div.head: C. Measurement of Interference Effects
div.p: In our experiments, we chose one of the cores to represent the application (called the application core) and the rest of the cores to represent the interfering load. We also chose thread execution times in such a way that each core's baseline utilization (execution time divided by period) is approximately 60%, consistent with prevailing engineering practice.

As each additional core is loaded, the application core's observed utilization increases since the execution times of the threads within the application increase with cache interference. The observed utilization of the application core therefore provides a direct measure of the interference when other cores are executing and sharing the last-level cache. Since it is desirable to maintain the total avionics application utilization well under 90%, we could then identify safe operating regions in the parameter space by tracking the observed application core utilization.

Following is the data processing method used to obtain the observed application core utilization under interference: Data processing: Each experiment was executed for 10 seconds of application time -hence collecting 600 samples of each of the 60 Hz threads, for example. For each thread in each experiment, the nTrace and nForge analysis used the LTTng trace log files to compute the execution time for each sample by identifying and filtering out the preemption times from the duration. Statistical data were extracted from the sample execution times thus calculated to arrive at average, minimum and maximum execution times of all samples in the experiment. Average sample execution time divided by the thread period was then used to compute the observed average utilization for that experiment. The notional maximum and minimum 'utilizations' were also computed using the maximum and minimum of samples in each experiment.

div.head: A. Visualizing Interference Effects
div.p: To understand how the baseline application core utilization increases with various parameters described above, it is important to visualize the high dimensional data effectively. We used the following chart types to visualize the results. Each point in the charts below represents one experiment.

Figure 3 depicts a 3-dimenional slice through our interference measurements for the 8-core Intel Xeon D-1541 processor. The graph shows Core 0 execution times increasing as more cores execute code competing for L3 cache space. As Core 0's ability to maintain its cache lines in L3 degrades, its execution time goes up, indicating more frequent waits for main memory to satisfy data references. Specifically in Figure 3, we plot application core utilization (in Z axis), as each core is loaded (in X axis), while studying its sensitivity to a 3rd parameter (in Y axis) -in this case, the read-write mix. This 3D graph has been colored to visualize the safe operating regions within this slice of the parameter space. Other parameters must be fixed at some values, which can later be varied for each rendering of the chart.

Although it provides a quick and intuitive way of visualizing safe operating regions, the data trends in the above chart can be better understood in Figure 4, which is a series of 2-dimensional slices along each of the values in the Y axis for the read-write mix. Note that the colors in this chart correspond to each value of read-write mix while the colors in the previous chart correspond to utilization.

As the interference cores are loaded, the utilization of the application core increases. The trend in slopes of each of the lines is illustrative of the impact of the increasing read-write mix. The all-read case is relatively less sensitive to interference effects, as can be seen by its slightly lower slope. It should be noted that this chart does not offer a valid way to compare the performances of each of the read-write mix cases. For example, the all-write case takes more time to execute than others.

However, since the baseline execution times have been adjusted such that each of them generate roughly 60% utilization in the no-interference case, we are only comparing the relative inference effects through the slopes of these lines.

div.head: B. Memory Utilization Parameter Sensitivity
div.p: In the parameter sensitivity tests, we used symmetric loads across all the cores in the system. That is, one data point represents the same load being placed on each core, both in CPU time and aggregate memory usage. We measure the application core utilization (which is a proxy for execution time) under the same nominal load with parameter variations and interference core loading. These charts show the interference effects of varying one parameter when all other parameters are held constant. Unless otherwise specified, the other parameters were held constant at the values specified in Table 2. Figure 4 shows the change in application core utilization with loading, with the data series indicating changing readwrite mix. The performance of the all-write case is significantly different from that of the all-read case. However, the impact of cache interference (which is exactly what Figure 4 highlights), on each of these cases is fairly similar. There is no significant difference in the slopes of these lines across the valid range of read-write mix. Hence, we concluded that this parameter has relatively small impact on cache interference for this platform.

Figure 5 shows the change in application core utilization with progressive core loading. The different data series, shown in different colors, represent differing aggregate application memory usage. The memory size has significant impact on the cache interference. At 8 MB per core application memory size, and with all of the 8 cores loaded, the Last Level Cache (LLC) of 12 MB is fairly saturated. Consequently, the increases in thread execution times force the application core utilization to exceed the total available processor capacity. Figure 7 shows the change in application core utilization with progressive core loading, with the data series, shown in different colors, indicating changing memory usage intensity. Since there is no significant difference across the valid range of memory usage intensity, we concluded that this parameter has relatively small impact on the cache interference.

Figure 8 shows the change in application core utilization with loading, with the data series indicating changing direction mix. There is no significant difference in slopes of these lines across the valid range of memory access direction mix. This would indicate that for the platform under experimentation, the caching algorithm does not significantly favor the memory read-ahead strategy over other data access methods. Therefore, we concluded that this parameter has relatively small impact on cache interference for this processor.

The experimental results for the application memory usage pattern presented above indicate a significant interference effect from application memory usage and not so significant effects from other memory usages parameters. Therefore, for the Xeon D-1541 processor under investigation, we concluded that the most important memory usage parameter for cache interference is the application's aggregate memory use.

div.head: C. Sensitivity to Processor Speed
div.p: The experiments with different processor speeds were more complex. We configured the hardware to use the chosen fixed processor speed, reset the processor, and then we repeated all the above experiments for each chosen speed. Figure 9 illustrates the effect of processor speed under progressive core loading. While the slopes of the lines may show a small increase with speed, the change is not significant. It can therefore be concluded that the processor speed is not a significant determinant of the cache interference for this platform.

div.head: D. Processor Utilization Parameter Sensitivity
div.p: In our experiments, the processor utilization pattern of the applications is defined by two parameters: application thread frequency and number of threads. Note that in our experiments, we hold the nominal (no-interference) load approximately at 60%, hence the execution times of these threads can be calculated. Figure 10 shows the effect of changing the number of threads, while holding other memory utilization parameters of the application the same. Specifically, when the total memory used by the application is held constant, say at 8 MB, increasing the number of threads in the application increases the fragmentation of the total application memory, and each of the threads step through smaller amount of memory. With the pseudo Least Recently Used (LRU) caching algorithm commonly used in multicore cache management, this fragmentation may allow for competing cores to hold a smaller total amount of memory in the last-level cache at any one instant in time. This phenomenon may explain why increasing the number of threads reduces the cache interference.

In addition to the average values, we also plotted the minimum and maximum bounds for the interference, expressed through minimum and maximum application core utilization. These are shown by dashed lines for minimum and dotted lines for maximum in Figure 10. The variance of interference can be seen to increase with number of threads, as illustrated by the width of the respective bands around the solid lines. Also, the fragmentation advantage for higher number of threads virtually disappears when considering the maximum interference, as shown by the dotted lines closer together than the solid lines.

Figure 11 shows the effect of varying application frequency on interference. It should be noted that all other parameters, notably the memory size and base utilization, are held constant. Hence a low frequency thread must loop through the same memory size more times to maintain the same baseline utilization, and therefore experiences increased execution time. In Figure 11, the variance can be seen as not as high as when the number of threads were being changed. Secondly, lowering the application frequency can be seen as reducing the effect of interference. This may appear contrary to the fragmentation effect we previously illustrated with increased number of threads.

However, a different effect may explain this observation. For example, reducing the frequency of application threads (while holding the total memory used by the application and the number of threads in the application the same) will result in higher residence times of the memory used by the application. Although the total memory demanded in the LLC is the same at any point in the execution for both high and low frequency cases, the number of frames in which the LLC needs to be refreshed is higher in the case of high frequency application threads. This leads to increased execution times experienced by the high frequency threads. Figure 12 shows when an application composed of mixed frequencies. In this experiment, a third of the threads were executed at 60 Hz, 30 Hz and 15 Hz. This caused slightly less interference than the all 60 Hz case, as can be expected. However, this results in a large variation around the average utilization, as can be seen from the width of the bands enclosed by dotted and dashed lines around the solid line.

div.head: E. Fixed Cache Allocation Results
div.p: Reference [11] describes the Intel Cache Allocation Technology (CAT), which can help address shared resource concerns by providing software control over where data is allocated into the last-level cache (LLC), enabling isolation and prioritization of key applications. This technology is meant for the allocation of cache to a limited number of key applications. However, the underlying mechanisms allow dedicating LLC regions to cores. For example, instead of 8 cores sharing the 12 MB LLC, each core can be allocated 1 or 2 MB of LLC dedicated to itself. In a set of experiments, we explored if the use of this mechanism improved system predictability under an overload condition.

When each core is allocated only a fixed region of cache, but uses memory in excess of that fixed space, its performance will understandably degrade. In the following experiment, we adjusted for this degradation via calibration for the nointerference case. The calibrated load was then placed in all 8 cores progressively to observe how the system behaves under memory overload. Figure 6 showed the baseline case with the CAT turned off, with the parameter values set as defined in Table 2.

CAT was then deployed by allocating 12 cache-ways of the processor to the 8 cores as follows: each of the 8 cores was allocated one dedicated cache-way. Each of the remaining 4 cache-ways was then shared between a pair of cores. Figure 13 presents the results in this setting. Even with the calibration of the no-interference baseline case adjusting for the lower performance of the restricted cache region use, this strategy performs worse under processor memory subset overload when other interfering cores come online. We expect this is due to other components of the processor memory subsystem also being shared among the cores.

The effect of CAT can be seen by the slight improvement, especially in the minimum utilization, when an adjacent core is left idle. When an adjacent core is in the pair of sharing cores left idle, the effective cache reservation for the loaded core has effectively doubled.

In conclusion, while CAT may be useful to manage specific high-memory key applications, it is not useful for establishing upper bounds for cache interference in a general avionics application use-case, even with the degraded baseline performance.

div.head: VI. APPLICATION IN PRACTICE
div.p: We anticipate that real-time practitioners may apply the results or methodology of this work to their systems in the following ways.

div.head: A. Formulaic Estimates for the Interference Bounds
div.p: The parametric sensitivity results presented in Section V.B can be further simplified based on the observations noted for this platform. Assuming that the applications executing on this processor platform use threads no faster than 60 Hz, and include at least 6 threads executing on each core, we can establish that the memory size used per core is the largest determinant of the cache interference. The effect of memory size on interference was shown previously in Figure 5.

If we assume a linear relationship of application core utilization (u) with the number of interference cores (ξ), we can approximate the application core utilization with the function shown in (1), given a baseline, no-interference utilization (B), and some function ψ of memory size μ .

For our experimentation platform and application assumptions, B = 60. From the results in Figure 5, the function ψ(μ) can be approximated to be μ/2. Thus we get: While this expression provides a quick way to estimate the application core utilization in the presence of cache interference, the entire dataset from the experiment results can be used in an interpolation scheme to obtain a better empirical estimate.

div.head: B. Interference Bounds For Use In Schedulability Analysis
div.p: Single core schedulability analysis typically uses the principles of Rate-Monotonic Analysis to predict worst-case completion times (WCCT) given the application threads, their periods, priorities and worst-case execution times (WCET). WCET is typically measured in the lab, under a worst-case path for the application logic. For the multicore case, it should ideally be measured with no other cores loaded, and later adjusted. Since the cache sharing among cores does not use application priorities, an empirical adjustment is needed for the WCET of all threads (regardless of their application priority, or memory usage) when using multicore processors.

With the results obtained for this platform, the adjustment to the WCET can be calculated prior to applying RMA. This adjustment acts similarly to that of a linear scaling for processing speed when adjusting execution times. The adjustment is based on aggregate memory consumed by each core, and the number of cores loaded. Based on the results in (2), a factor (f) to inflate each of the thread's WCET can be derived empirically for this experimentation platform:

The inflated WCET can then be used for schedulability analysis, to arrive at WCCT and the overall schedulability of the system. Application of (3) is based on the following assumptions on the target system: (i) uses the same processor platform as this experimentation, (ii) employs independent, harmonic, periodic threads with no data sharing, and (iii) uses an engineering practice of keeping the baseline no-interference loads for each core around 60%.

div.head: C. Trade-off Studies for Hardware Software Allocation
div.p: The results of this empirical study can be integrated into automated or manual methods of software to hardware allocation trade-offs. To facilitate this process, an automated tool can incorporate the interference model contained in this paper to adjust for, and predict cache interference effects when using multicore architectures. nForge is an example of such a software tool [13].

While actual measurements with integrated applications will always be the final step in systems design, initial evaluation of a specific allocation strategy can be useful to quickly establish its viability for multicore architectures.

div.head: D. Executable Interference Models
div.p: For a set of tasks with known memory usage patterns, and the ability to induce loads with those usage patterns on all the cores in the processor, it becomes easy to create integrated models of system execution. This gives system architects the ability to directly measure interference effects due to multicore cache usage. Further, these integrated models give the architects the ability to overestimate execution times and memory fingerprints, providing a methodology to build in safety margins. The extent of the overestimation is dependent on how homoegeneous the resource usage is among the cores. A balanced allocation of software applications to cores in practice will result in a relatively modest overestimation of the interference effects by this method.

The analogy is with building traffic bridges, where the bridge is designed to carry loads 2x-3x of estimated peak, with the margins dependent on environmental parameter variations within anticipated boundaries. Software automation (e.g., via nForge) allows for creating and analyzing these interference models, and for generating proxies that match application fingerprints for interference benchmarking and safety margins.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this experimental study, we explored the effect of multicore cache intereference on real-time schedulability under various parametric characteristics of applications and processor speed. We conclude that a reasonable high-confidence upper bound can be established under a set of assumptions common to avionics practice -independent, periodic, harmonic tasks with no data sharing and no dynamic memory use.

The empirically established upper bound is based on thorough exercise of loading possibilities by varying relevant parameters so as to produce resource saturation and capture respective threshold combinations. Hence, the results can be used with high confidence in certification for operation of applications that are consistent with the assumptions made in this study.

For the specific platform used, we further conclude that the following application characteristics are the most relevant to cache interference: (i) memory size of applications, (ii) number of loaded cores, and (iii) the number of and frequency of threads that comprise an application. All of these characteristics can be readily estimated in a typical real-time avionics systems engineering environment.

div.head: VIII. FUTURE WORK
div.p: We used Real-Time Linux and associated tools for this experimental study. While the methodology is generic, this study needs to be repeated with the system's target hardware and software infrastructure in order to be readily applicable in practice.

In a multicore architecture, other hardware components may also be shared among cores. Examples include I/O channels and network hardware. Sharing these components and the supporting hardware elements may induce additional interference. Studies are needed to quantify and include them in analysis.

This study assumed a simplified generalized avionics application design with no data-sharing. Adjustments need to be made if data sharing and the resultant blocking and priority inversion avoidance techniques are used.

This study focused on establishing an upper bound on the interference effect for given engineering standards, using homogeneous, worst-case loading on all cores. This may prove to be pessimistic for the general case of hetrogenous loads on all cores. Studies are needed to establish realistic interference bounds, admittedly at the expense of combinatorial explosion of experimental parameters involving all cores.
